guidance: Reference for Japanese paperwork, product dates and correspondence, not an official registry record. The five eras since 1868 are fixed, but the page stops at Meiji because earlier eras ran on the lunisolar calendar and cannot be expressed as Gregorian months and days; use a historical calendar converter for those.
method: The page holds one table of the five eras used since 1868, each with its first civil year and the day it began and, where it has ended, the day of its last date: Meiji from 23 October 1868 to 29 July 1912, Taishō from 30 July 1912 to 24 December 1926, Shōwa from 25 December 1926 to 7 January 1989, Heisei from 8 January 1989 to 30 April 2019, and Reiwa from 1 May 2019. Since the Meiji era Japan has used one era name per reign, so the era year is simply the civil year minus the era's first year plus one: 1989 is Shōwa 64 until 7 January and Heisei 1 from 8 January, 1912 is Meiji 45 until 29 July and Taishō 1 from 30 July, and the year a new era opens is known as its gannen, written 元年, which the page reports alongside the numbered year. A date is placed by its own day rather than by its year, so an era date is checked against the day the era began or ended and refused with that day when it falls outside: 8 January 1989 is not Shōwa 64, and 30 April 2019 is not Reiwa 1. Both directions go through one continuous count of civil days (1 January of year 1 is day 1), so the weekday (that count modulo 7, with day 1 a Monday), the day of the year and the round trip between the two forms cannot drift. The short form joins the era's initial to the era year, as in M45, S64, H31 and R8, the convention used in Japanese date stamps. When a civil year carries two era years the result names the other one, so 1989 reads "1989 also carries Shōwa 64" beside Heisei 1. Dates from 1 January 1873 (Meiji 6) to 31 December 2100 are supported, the span in which Japan has used the Gregorian calendar with its own months and days, so a Gregorian date before 1873 is refused instead of being labelled with a lunisolar era date. Every civil day in that window was compared with ICU's Japanese calendar (ja-JP-u-ca-japanese), 83,275 days, with no difference in era name, era year, month or day, and every date round-trips through the shared day count. Blank, malformed and out-of-range entries are refused with a field-specific message. The page makes no network request and stores nothing.

sources.title: Japanese era name: the five eras since 1868 with their start dates, the issei-ichigen one-era-per-reign rule, the gannen first year, and the conversion rule of civil year minus first year plus one
Japanese calendar: the 1873 (Meiji 6) adoption of the Gregorian calendar with its months and days, the lunisolar calendar used before it, and the year-month-day order of era dates
ICU date/time calendar guide: the Japanese calendar (ja-JP-u-ca-japanese) whose era names and era years were compared day by day against this page over 1873-2100, with no differences
